lines.watchItem: Merchant-GPU demand is running far ahead of supply this cycle, with record data-center sales and roughly $725B of hyperscaler spending planned for 2026. That gap keeps leading-edge wafer demand pointed sharply upward while the supply side stays tight.

Advanced packaging, not the wafer itself, is the tight point: CoWoS is booked out through 2027 with year-plus lead times, and it is named as the binding constraint on how much GPU revenue can actually ship. The gap is easing toward about 10% by end-2026 but stays short.
Packaging output is heavily tied to a handful of buyers: the top three CoWoS clients take over 85%, with one vendor near 60%. That concentration ties realizable output to a very small customer set.

Custom chips designed for the big cloud buyers are growing much faster than merchant GPUs and reportedly already run about two-thirds of AI compute. How the leading-node base splits between merchant GPUs and this custom silicon is shifting toward the custom side.

End-market pricing stays firm across the chain: foundry margins near 68%, lead-chip vendor margins at 75%, memory contract prices roughly doubling into 2027, and rental GPU prices up. Tight supply is holding pricing power in place for now.

Several competing accelerators are moving into mass production at once and a rival is expanding its own foundry capacity, while China exposure keeps eroding. These developments cut against the current lead and raise second-source and policy exposure around foundry demand.

Memory supply is its own choke point alongside packaging: HBM is sold out through 2027 with order books into 2028 and suppliers meeting only part of demand. Firm HBM availability bears directly on how much accelerator volume can be built.
